scholar: Daniel Boyarin (Jewish scholar, Talmud and early Judaism)
work: The Jewish Gospels: The Story of the Jewish Christ, 2012
chapter_or_section: Ch. 'From Son of God to Son of Man' / Mark 14 blasphemy passage (exact chapter not recovered; preview sequence PT102)
page: page unknown (Google Books preview id PT102; printed page not shown)
quote_orig: Even if eigo eimi is innocent, Jesus' further allusion to himself as the Son of Man and coming with the clouds of heaven certainly, according to the high priest's reaction, constitutes blasphemy and thus a claim to divine status.
context_before: Boyarin has just said that blasphemy means 'imputing divine status to oneself or to another human' (Philo) and that 'the blasphemy consists precisely in Jesus claiming divine status for himself.' The quote continues the same argument about the trial before the high priest.
what_it_says: Boyarin holds that, in Mark's trial scene, the Son of Man allusion (Dan 7:13) is a claim to divine status, as the high priest's reaction shows.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself claims divine identity, as Boyarin reads the Markan trial; partly (B), since the text is the Gospel narrative.
scholar_qualification: The claim is argued from the Gospel narrative (the high priest's reaction). Boyarin separates the 'I am' (eigo eimi) wording from the Son of Man allusion ('Even if ... is innocent'). On Mark 2:10 he says the Son of Man's forgiving authority is 'obviously delegated by God' (PT47), i.e., not God's own authority. Peter Schafer (New Republic, 2012) calls Boyarin's Daniel 7 reading 'a breathtaking hypothesis' and 'dubious' and says it 'erases' pre-Christian traditions. Another scholar's view, which Boyarin contests in the same passage, is cited only as 'her view' in the snippet; I did not identify her.

work: Der historische Jesus: Ein Lehrbuch (1996); English: The Historical Jesus: A Comprehensive Guide, 1998
edition: English: Fortress Press, 1998, ISBN 0800631226 (Google Books record). German 2023 edition: Wer war Jesus? (Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht), quoted by blog
chapter_or_section: 'Jesus as Son of Man: The Explicit Christology' (German 2023 ed. pp. 407-416, as quoted by blog)
page: 552 (English 1998 edition, as cited by the blog); German 2023: pp. 415-416
quote_orig: No angel, no heavenly being, no one who was only like a man, but a concrete man will take over his role in the kingdom of God which is breaking in: Jesus himself. He is at the same time the present and the future 'man'.
context_before: The authors write: 'In our view the interpretation mentioned last is therefore the most probable one: Jesus spoke of both the present and the future Son of Man.' They explain that he combined the everyday phrase 'son of man' with the heavenly 'like a son of man' of Daniel 7.
what_it_says: Theissen and Merz argue that Jesus understood himself as the present and future Son of Man, the one concrete figure who takes the heavenly role.
claim_supported: (A) partly: exalted self-consciousness and identity with a heavenly Son of Man figure, not explicit divinity; also (D) Second Temple background. The German term is 'Hoheitsbewusstsein' (consciousness of exalted status or majesty).
scholar_qualification: The authors call the interpretation 'most probable' in their view, and they state the difficulty: a person 'speaking about his own future as though about another person'. Their German wording 'Hoheitsbewusstsein' is about exalted status, not 'God'. In the 2023 German text they say Jesus was 'probably both' the candidate for the future Son of Man and the earthly representative of the present one. The 'divine' sense is not asserted in these lines.
source_type: other (blog that quotes the English 1998 text with page 552, and the German 2023 text with pp. 415-416)

quote_orig: the divine origin of her son was formulated in the land of Israel and not within the Hellenistic Church. We can no longer rule out the possibility that Jesus indeed would have regarded himself as the “son of God.”
context_before: Knohl ties the annunciation language (Gabriel's words about the child) to Qumran texts, and argues that the idea of a divine origin for the child 'was formulated in the land of Israel'. The quote is his conclusion on the 'son of God' title.
what_it_says: Knohl says it can no longer be ruled out that the historical Jesus regarded himself as 'son of God', in the sense of the Qumran royal-messianic figure.
claim_supported: (A) hedged: a possibility, not an assertion. (D) Second Temple room for a divine-sonship figure.
scholar_qualification: Knohl writes 'can no longer rule out the possibility'. He says that if Jesus did claim the Son of Man role, 'why did he not refer to himself directly ... but only indirectly, as the “son of man”?' (p.2). He writes 'Perhaps the historical Jesus really did see himself in this way' (p.26, about the Son of Man-suffering servant fusion). His 'son of God' is a royal-messianic figure, not a claim to identity with YHWH.

work: Review of Daniel Boyarin, The Jewish Gospels: 'The Jew Who Would Be God'
chapter_or_section: Review, section on Daniel 7 and the Son of God
page: not applicable (magazine review, no page numbers)
quote_orig: This is a breathtaking hypothesis. As to the Son of God, Boyarin contents himself with the (correct) reference to some passages according to which the biblical Messiah is the Davidic king of Israel, who is clearly a human figure. Yet with a stroke of his pen Boyarin erases all the pre-Christian Jewish traditions in which the Son of God means much more than just a human king,
context_before: Schafer summarizes Boyarin's thesis: 'the appellation “Son of God” refers to the Messiah as a king, whereas the appellation “Son of Man” ... refers to the divine redeemer'.
what_it_says: Schafer says Boyarin's reading erases pre-Christian Jewish traditions in which 'Son of God' means more than a human king, and he calls Boyarin's Daniel 7 reading 'breathtaking' and dubious.
claim_supported: (D) background: he affirms that pre-Christian Jewish 'Son of God' could mean more than a human king, and rejects Boyarin's reading of the Son of Man as divine.
scholar_qualification: Schafer rejects Boyarin's binitarian Daniel 7 reading, saying the angel's interpretation and Michael reading are more likely. He does not discuss Jesus' own claims at length in this review. He accepts the New Testament's divine Son of God passages (Romans 1:3-4, Philippians 2) as a separate matter he does not dispute.
source_type: other (online magazine review, The New Republic, May 18, 2012)
